summary: This document sets which cryptographic algorithms IPsec implementations must, should, or should not support for ESP and AH, the protocols that encrypt and authenticate IP traffic. It also adds guidance on choosing among them. It was replaced by RFC 8221.

plainLanguage.summary: Two friends need a secret code to pass notes. This RFC lists which codes every notebook must know, which are nice to have, and which are too weak. It has since been replaced by a newer list.

questions: which algorithms must ipsec esp support
when should i use authenticated encryption
subtitle: Choose strong encryption algorithms for IPsec protocols

tldr.problem: IPsec implementations must agree on which cryptographic algorithms to support, but cryptographic algorithms weaken over time and new ones emerge. A standard list prevents implementations from choosing algorithms that are too weak.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines which algorithms are mandatory, recommended, optional, or forbidden for use in ESP and AH protocols, and provides guidance on selecting among them.
tldr.outcome: IPsec implementations can interoperate while avoiding broken algorithms. The RFC was replaced by RFC 8221, which updated the recommendations.

today: RFC 7321 is still a Proposed Standard for IPsec algorithm requirements. It was obsoleted by RFC 8221 in 2017, which updated the recommendations to reflect developments in cryptography.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH) are IPsec mechanisms that add cryptographic protection to IP packets. They encrypt data for confidentiality and add authentication checks to verify data has not been tampered with. To ensure different implementations can talk to each other, they must support a common set of algorithms.

This RFC specifies which algorithms MUST be implemented, which SHOULD be implemented (likely to become mandatory later), which are optional, and which MUST NOT be used because they are too weak. It also provides guidance on choosing between algorithms to achieve different security goals.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers need to agree on codes. This tells which codes every computer must know, which are good to learn, which you can skip, and which are broken.

sections.title: Algorithm Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC categorizes algorithms with these levels: MUST means all implementations are required to support it; SHOULD+ means likely to become mandatory later; SHOULD and MAY are optional but recommended; MUST NOT means too weak and forbidden.

For ESP authenticated encryption (combined encryption and authentication in one algorithm), AES-GCM with 16-byte integrity check is SHOULD+, meaning implementations are encouraged to add it soon. For encryption alone, NULL (no encryption) and AES-CBC are MUST; AES-CTR and TripleDES are optional; DES-CBC is forbidden. For authentication alone, HMAC-SHA1-96 is required, while AES-GMAC and AES-XCBC-MAC are recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: Some codes everyone must know, some are strongly recommended, some are okay to skip, and some are too broken to use.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC advises on combining these algorithms. The best security comes from using authenticated encryption, which encrypts data and adds an authentication check in one operation. If you only need authentication without encryption, use AES-GMAC or HMAC-SHA1-96, with the community preferring ESP with NULL encryption over AH. Never use encryption without authentication; encryption alone creates a false sense of security.

TripleDES is discouraged because it is a 64-bit block cipher and becomes unsafe when encrypting large amounts of data with the same key. DES is completely forbidden because its 56-bit key and 64-bit blocks are computationally breakable today.
sections.plainLanguage: Best: encrypt and check at the same time. Okay: just check. Never: encrypt without checking. Old codes like TripleDES should not be used.

sections.title: Why These Choices
sections.content:
AES-GCM is promoted because it offers both encryption and authentication efficiently, with performance benefits on modern hardware. It has become the preferred method in IPsec and other standards. AES-CBC with a separate authentication algorithm remains required for backward compatibility but is less efficient than combined algorithms.

TripleDES was kept as optional for legacy systems but its small block size makes it unsafe at high data rates. DES is completely forbidden because its small key size makes it vulnerable to exhaustive search attacks and special-purpose hardware has been built to break it. The RFC recommends avoiding TripleDES and DES entirely in new systems.
sections.plainLanguage: AES-GCM is fast and secure. Old codes like TripleDES are slow and weak. DES is completely broken.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of IPsec depends on both the strength of the algorithms chosen and the strength of the keys used with those algorithms. The algorithms marked MUST or SHOULD in this RFC are not known to be broken and are believed to remain secure for the foreseeable future.

However, cryptography continuously evolves. New weaknesses may be discovered in currently recommended algorithms, and new algorithms may emerge. This RFC will need to be updated over time to reflect advances in cryptographic research. Implementers should expect that today's recommended algorithms may become deprecated in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Strong algorithms can become weak if researchers discover attacks. That is why the rules for which codes to use will change over time.
